strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First rigorous analysis of transfer learning with feature learning in both source and target tasks in infinite-width networks
Technically rigorous framework using statistical mechanics (replica trick, saddle point equations) with complete proofs
Excellent experimental validation: Theory predictions match DMFT simulations across linear, polynomial, and real datasets
Rich insights about transfer learning dynamics: reveals non-trivial trade-offs between elastic coupling, feature learning strength, and task similarity
Complementary theoretical perspectives: both Bayesian and gradient flow analyses provide independent validation
Clear presentation: well-organized despite technical complexity, with detailed appendices
Insightful phenomenology: identifies when transfer helps/hurts and mechanisms driving these effects
weaknesses: Restricted to two-layer networks: modern deep learning uses much deeper architectures; extension to depth unclear and severely limits practical relevance
Significant gap between theory and practice: elastic penalty δ||W - W̄||² is somewhat artificial; real transfer learning uses learning rate scheduling; mean-field parameterization not standard
Limited real-world experiments: only CIFAR-10 tested, only binary classification (2 classes per task); no experiments on standard transfer scenarios or with 10-way classification
No dataset averaging: theoretical equations scale with P₂, limiting predictive power for different dataset sizes; acknowledged limitation not addressed
Lack of practical guidance: no clear method to choose δ in practice; relationship to standard transfer learning hyperparameters unclear; no comparison with LoRA, adapters, or standard fine-tuning
Limited statistical rigor: missing error bars, confidence intervals, and significance tests on most experimental results; no ablation studies on key design choices
Incomplete technical justification: replica-symmetric ansatz assumed valid without rigorous justification; validity of mean-field limit for P₂ = O(N) not established
Methodology specificity: elastic coupling δ||W - W̄||² is one choice; alternatives not explored; only squared loss analyzed; sensitivity to architectural choices not studied

strengths: Develops novel theoretical framework for transfer learning in infinite-width networks with feature learning in both phases, extending prior work limited to fixed kernels or lazy learning
Comprehensive multi-scale analysis from general deep networks (Result 1) to explicit closed-form linear models (Results 2-4) with clear phase diagrams characterizing when transfer succeeds
Rigorous technical work: DMFT dynamics, path integral derivations, and careful limiting analysis appear sound; validated through Monte Carlo DMFT simulations and experiments

Clear interpretable insights: Results show how data quantity (ν₁, ν₂), task alignment (α), and feature learning strength (γ₁, γ₂) control transfer success; identifies regimes of positive transfer, negative transfer via noise crosstalk, and feature collapse
Exceptional technical depth: Thorough appendices with DMFT primer, detailed proofs, Bayesian extension, and multiple experimental settings (synthetic tasks, CIFAR-10, MNIST)
weaknesses: Severely limited practical applicability: infinite-width limit without finite-width error bounds, gradient flow instead of SGD, mean-field parameterization (µP) non-standard in practice, isotropic Gaussian data assumption; theory operates in regime distant from modern practice

Incomplete analysis of key results: Result 3 (finite-data effects) leaves coefficients c₁, c₂, c₃ implicit, only solved via DMFT saddle points (Appendix C.2); the ansatz (Eq. 11) is phenomenological, not rigorously derived. Deep networks beyond 2-layer lack detailed analysis

Restrictive assumptions throughout: all closed-form results assume isotropic covariance or linear/polynomial targets; real data structured; balance condition in Result 4 assumes specific initialization not discussed; random initialization arguments require large N without quantitative rates

Gap between theory and experiments: CIFAR-10 experiments use only 2 source + 2 target classes; ansatz for polynomial tasks (Fig. 2a) is phenomenological extrapolation, not rigorous. No standard baselines or comparison to existing transfer learning methods

Incremental methodological novelty: DMFT, path integrals, and Hubbard transforms are established; main novelty is application to transfer learning. Bayesian NN extension (Appendices E-F) uses different assumptions and feels disconnected

Dense presentation reducing accessibility: Results 1-4 stated formally without plain-language motivation; key derivations in appendix; connection between results and actionable insights unclear. Result 1 too complex for practical guidance; Results 2-4 restricted to linear models

Missing practical guidance: no recommendations for choosing γ₁, γ₂ beyond theoretical phase diagrams; no finite-width analysis to bridge theory-practice gap; no extension to CNNs, attention, or modern architectures; limited guidance on when theory applies
